source.title: Over-Parameterization and Generalization in Audio Classification
source.authors: Khaled Koutini; Hamid Eghbalzadeh; Florian Henkel; Jan Schlüter; G. Widmer

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps CNN width and depth and reports test accuracy, bearing on model-size/generalization behavior in an audio-classification setting. It does not directly measure the full double-descent curve or its interpolation peak.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for width, depth, and sparsified-width sweeps. Training-set fit and random-label fit are capacity checks, not test-error results, so they are not rows. Prior studies' results cited in the text are not included.
record.test_reason: Audio scene classification is a new setting. The baseline (W=32) already fits the training set at 99.99%, so every width and depth sweep sits past the interpolation threshold. Test accuracy versus model size there bears on V1's second-descent part only. The under-parameterized fall and the peak are never sampled.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly right. Widening CNNs gives the largest unseen-device generalization gain, even where seen-device gains are absent and even at fixed parameter count. Depth scaling can worsen unseen-device performance. The results are interpreted through the effective receptive field. The authors do not claim to test double descent.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales audio-classification CNNs by width and depth and evaluates device-domain generalization; it does not reproduce the original double-descent experiments or measure a peak around interpolation.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes differ with scaling method (width versus depth, including 3×3 versus 1×1 blocks), receptive-field damping, and seen versus unseen recording devices. In sparse-width tests, static random pruning and iterative magnitude pruning differ.

fits_no_version.finding: At a parameter count fixed to the W=64 model, widening via static random pruning gives initial unseen-device gains that diminish at larger widths. Iterative magnitude pruning shows a minimal unseen-device drop even at 98.4% sparsity, while the damped model drops on the seen device.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At fixed parameter count, widening audio CNNs can improve unseen-device generalization, with the effect depending on the pruning method.

record.peer_reviewed: Presented at the ICML 2021 Workshop on Overparameterization: Pitfalls & Opportunities
record.problems: The results concern one audio-classification dataset and a device-mismatch evaluation, not a general test-error setting. Most sweep values are presented in figures rather than stated numerically; although the paper says it repeats experiments 3 times and reports the mean and standard deviation of the last 10 epochs, numerical uncertainty values are not given in the extracted text.
record.rows_left_out: No separately described test-performance results bearing on the claim were left out. The paper also presents effective-receptive-field plots, but those are mechanistic measurements rather than test-error results for the listed versions.

untested.parts: The under-parameterized fall and the test-error peak at the interpolation threshold. The smallest model (W=32) already interpolates, so only the post-threshold regime is sampled.
All; there is no epoch-wise test-error analysis.
All; sample size is not varied.
All; label noise and regularization tuning are not varied.

missing.what: Interpolation location: W=32 fits training data at 99.99% and random labels at 85.51%; W=64 fits random labels at 100%. Every sweep is therefore past the threshold, which a comparer needs to interpret the rows.

Test accuracy versus number of parameters across width, depth and RF-preserving depth scaling, for Damped (Fig. 1) and base ResNet (Fig. 17). Width scaling clearly beats depth at matched parameter counts.

record.verdict_notes: The study cites the double-descent originals but does not probe the peak. Its relevance is limited to post-interpolation behaviour in one dataset (TAU Urban Acoustic Scenes 2020 Mobile). The depth declines are attributed to receptive-field growth, a task-specific inductive-bias effect rather than variance. Runs use 3 seeds with mean and standard deviation shown only in figures. Mixup augmentation is used throughout and acts as a regularizer.

versions.untested_parts: It does not establish an initial fall, a peak near the interpolation threshold, and a second fall across a complete model-size range; it also does not report training-set fit alongside each test result to locate that threshold.
No test-error sweep over training epochs is reported.
Training-set sample size is not varied.
The study tests CNN scaling in one audio-classification setting, not the general double-descent curve across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is used to predict peak locations across axes.
The paper does not test whether noise drives a peak, whether multiple peaks occur, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes a peak.
The study does not re-express the results using an effective parameter count or test whether that yields an ordinary U-shaped curve.
